text: The company runs Dev, Test, and Production instances for Equipment Checkout, the scoped application the Scripting & Application Development capstone built, with its checkout table extending task for its approval lifecycle and its standalone equipment table holding static inventory data.

It's been live in Production for a full quarter, and two things are landing at once: the quarterly sub-production refresh is due, and the team is about to ship a significant new feature, an Overdue Checkouts module with automatic escalation, already built and tested in Dev and Build. Walk through both, in the right order, the way a real admin and developer would plan it.

Step one: plan the refresh. Dev and Test haven't been refreshed since launch, so their data is a quarter stale, missing real checkout patterns and real equipment categories added since launch, plus real edge cases, like equipment checked out and never returned, that now only exist in Production. The plan clones current checkout and equipment data from Production into Dev and Test on the scheduled quarterly date, the same way any application's refresh would run.

Step two: that clone carries real employee data along with it, every real name and contact detail tied to a requested-for or assignment field on a real checkout record. Before any developer or tester is allowed to open the refreshed instance, anonymization runs against those fields, permanently replacing real values with realistic fake ones, exactly the way Security & Access Controls described. Nobody testing the new escalation logic needs a real employee's real email address to confirm a notification fires correctly.

Step three: separately, before the Overdue Checkouts feature ships, the team publishes a new Application Repository version of Equipment Checkout, capturing the entire application including the new module as one coherent, numbered snapshot, instead of relying on tracking which specific Update Sets collectively represent the app before this feature. That published version becomes the clean rollback point if the new logic misbehaves once it's live.

This lab combined every real idea from this chapter: recognizing that sub-production needs periodic refreshing to stay realistic, treating anonymization as a required step in that refresh rather than an afterthought, and publishing a version at a real milestone so a coherent rollback point exists if it's needed.

Refresh, then anonymize, then version before release — that sequence is exactly what a real ServiceNow team running a real application does every quarter, not a one-time exercise. Next, Chapter 2 opens with Update Set batching strategies at scale.
